Good morning.
Good morning.
How are you doing?
Very well.
How are you?
I'm good, thank you.
Lesley, good.
You looking well.
Thank you.
Hello.
Good morning.
How are you?
Good to meet you.
Good to meet you too, Stan.
Thank you.
Hi, Stan.
How you doing?
Are you all right?
I arrived.
Okay, so where you.
Are you someplace exotic or where are you?
Who me?
Yeah, I'm at Liverpool train station, which is a big, big train station in London.
Got it.
So I'm just kind of in, in between meetings with you guys.
I've just met an old client actually, whose company I sold last year, based in, in Los Angeles to a company in New York.

Sure, sure.
So, Leslie, my background, I was formerly a journalist, worked for the New York Times as a reporter, ABC News, is a producer.

And then I went over to the deep dark other side of PR and went to Burson, Marsteller, Fleischmann, Hillard and Edelman and over a 20 year period ran different business units and geographies for those firms.
So at Burson, I started as the head of corporate in Miami.
It then extended to Latin America.
And then, and then I ran their Anderson Consulting business globally for them.
At Fleischman I was President of the Middle East.
And also, I mean, I never, never was able to shake professional service.
So I ran their Deloitte business globally as well.
And then at Edelman, I ran a change management practice for Richard Edelman and he and I work closely together.
I took a in house position at a company called Armstrong holdings, which was the flooring and ceiling manufacturer.

And you know, as I think many of us in our business, we all have this, we think it's going to be romantic on the corporate side until you get there and you know, you find out that instead of being in the center of the action, you're a service to the guys who really make the money, which I didn't find terribly appealing.
So, you know, I did, I did stay there for three years, but then really left and started this business Here.
So today we're 110 people.
We have nine offices around the world.
It's a somewhat diversified practice.
I'd say that some of our core is consumer products, specifically home furnishings.
We're the largest agency in the country with that.
So it's everything from mattresses and everything that goes into mattresses to sofas, including retailers.
So we do work for Bloomingdale's, for example, as well.
Macy's on and off again.
So, you know, so that's a pretty diverse practice.
And again, sort of consumer products represents about 30% of our business.
We certainly do a lot of tech, a lot of finance.
Fintech has been a big area for us.
We also, because of some strategic positioning we did.
We're.
We have a very large practice in Israel and in the Gulf.
We in Trump won.
And this isn't my political affiliation.
I don't know where you stand in things, but in Trump, 1.
Jared Kushner is somebody who we knew very well before the Abraham Accords were established.
They sort of recommended, well, hey, you guys have, you know, you have an office in Tel Aviv, but you got nothing in Dubai.
You may want to think about that.
And we, we took them up on that, and it really opened a tremendous amount of business for us because no other agency, even the large ones, didn't have both Israel and the Gulf.
So it opened up a lot of channels for us, and that's become a big practice for us.
We also do a fair amount of government work around the world, again, all different types of governments.
And we also have a business and defense, which has become sort of an emerging segment for us primarily.
And I think, interestingly enough, that warfare is becoming very tech oriented.
So kind of an outgrowth of our technology.
There's a lot of unmanned vehicles, drones, and things like that being developed today.
So we're becoming more of a player in that space as well.
So anyway, at 50,000ft, and it may be more than two minutes, so I apologize, but that's kind of an overview of who we are.
Well, thank you for that.
I can call you Stan, presumably.
Please, please, yeah.
Please call me Leslie.
I'm in the south, so it's terribly formal.
Well, I'm a business owner and I'm from London, and clients never guess how I vote on both sides of the pond, as I have both national, I have both passports because I have clients on all spectrums.
But you can figure it out if we get to know each other.
Anyway, all that to say, which of your offices are you in this morning?
I know I've obviously heard of you before and looked at your website and everything.
You've got a very impressive backgr background and you know, your company does great things.
Where are you primarily based?
Well, so.
So New Jersey or northern New Jersey has become our base.
We after Covid.
Covid was.
It was very difficult.
We were based in Manhattan exclusively and we had finance and ops in North Jersey.
We had a very small office here.
But what happened is the suburbs opened up really more than the city did.
So I couldn't get anybody to go into the city.
So we all kind of camped out here.
People liked it here.
Even the people that commuted from Manhattan liked it here.
So when we had the opportunity to get out of our lease in the city, we kept a small office there just so that we can do meetings and things like that.
But North Jersey is really kind of our headquarters, let's call it for us.
So that's where I am today.
Okay, good to know.
So my background is, as you can probably guessed from the accent, I'm from London.
I actually my first job was in.
At Edelman.
They call it an internship now, but it was back in the day.
It was a summer job while I was at Bristol Uni.
And I've always been an agency junkie.
I've loved the change.
And I know what you're saying about the in house.
Having worked with a lot of in house marketing people, I kind of knew it wasn't for me.
So I worked my way up.
I had a graduate traineeship with a Saatch group that you might remember back in the day was, you know, a big deal and I worked my way up.
In 1998 I decided to go to go it alone and I set up my first agency with nothing.
And I built that over the course of nine years to a top 15 in healthcare.
I specialized in healthcare.
I saw that as a niche.
I saw medical devices was not being given the attention that pharmaceuticals were back in the UK at that time.

I obviously, you know, because you're international, the rules regarding promotion and prescription products are very different in the UK to the US And I had had a lot of experience in healthcare with the Shire Hall Group.
So I set that up and grew that over the years.
In 2007 I had about 20 employees.
I felt that I got it as far as I could as an independent and I took the opportunity to sell to a company that it's now part of, Dentsu, many years.
So I sold in 2007.
Of course, I don't know Any marketing agency that made their numbers, we certainly didn't.
We carried on, but we didn't make our numbers.
So I did my year.
I was committed to a year.
And I'll be very honest with you, in some ways it was great with Jaro Slipstream as it was then, and actually spent some time in Dubai setting operations there.
But I didn't, it wasn't what I thought it would be, if I'm very honest.
And I did my year and I thought, you know, it's time for me to have another phase now.
My husband's American and we have family here.
Took the chance to come to the U.S.
enjoyed both weeks of my retirement.
I was still in my very early 40s.
Started doing some freelancing after a couple of years in 2011, I thought, okay, I'm going to have to set up another agency.

As I'm sure you're aware.
The greater Savannah area, port and tourism and Hyundai down the road.
So built that again from scratch and have a team.
We diversified a little over the years.
I called it Lesley Francis, Public relations now lfpr.

But having grown and obviously with the digitalization of communications and all the changes we've seen in the media, I now have graphic designer, social media, web development and that's obviously a growth area with AI coming in.
So, yeah.
So really looking at the opportunities.
What's the next step?
How can I, you know, what's the, what's the next step for me and my career?
I'm 59, but I'm only 59.
How can I offer my team and my clients the edge that they've come to expect?
And honestly, we spoke to Andy and you know, let's explore opportunities.
I'm delighted to meet with you this morning.
Super, super.
So.
So a couple of things, you know, again, top line and if, you know, if we go to a second or third date, we'll, we'll get deeper into the details.
But how many people do you have now on staff?
There are five full time staff and I also have an intern program.
I pay them a little.
We are accredited by the University of Georgia and Georgia Southern and that is actually helpful.
And I have a website developer and I have some freelancers that I rely on on a 1099 basis, but I have five salaried staff.
Got it.
And so plus me.
I apologize.
Go ahead.
Yeah.
And by.

But who, who do you consider your sort of number two?

And I've mentored them.
My vp Kristen and she's actually been years.
There's a lot of loyalty and I've always enjoyed mentoring.

Is it a fee basis?
Hourly.
How do you do that?
Retainer.

Not every client buys every service.
So once I'm in there.
Oh, so like Telfair museums, they, they've lost a person that we do media relations, great relationship.
Oh, I now need you to do another service.
So that is often a way in.
But I would say over 90% of our clients, it's all fee based and it is retainer.
We have annual contract.
Occasionally I'll do a project with a minimum of three months.
About half the time that turns into a retainer or additional project.
But that's very much the model.
Got it.
And give me a range on retainer.
Yeah, I mean this, remember this isn't New York or London and it really depends on the services they purchase.
But I mean it can be anything from, you know, from 3,000 for you know, a smaller client.
We do offer a discount to non profits.
I'm moving away a little bit from that of 20% of our bill available time is given to non profits.

That's something that, it's getting a little old and with the, the problems in terms of grant funding and also in terms of the Donor base actually moving away a little from that model, then through to 9 or 10,000amonth.
It really is a big range.
And remember, as I say, we're a small agency in a small.
The salaries are not what they are in New York or London.
Yeah, no, look, you know, and I'll tell you, just so you kind of understand some of my thinking, we do what I kind of call fair billing.
Okay?
So we have.
Okay, not for profits, that are paying 2500.
Okay, and 3500.
What I tell my team, you know, each employee, for cost accounting purposes, has an hourly rate.
And what I tell them is when we go out, we do new business, you build your program and what's it going to cost?
And if it's going to cost 2500, then that's what we're going to go in with.
We're not going to play games of how much can we get out of the client.
Because to be very, you know, be very honest with you, our average client is with us 12.
We've been in business for 22 years.
Our average client is with us 12 to 13 years.
We have many that go back 20 and 21 years.
So, you know, I want to.
We make money the longer we keep a client, okay?
So I don't want to play games, you know, like that.
And so, you know, people are.
They're shocked because, you know, in the furniture business, for example, we do a lot of work in North Carolina or South Carolina.
And, you know, people immediately think, well, because we're based in the Northeast, the fees are going to be crazy and ridiculous.
And when we actually tell them what it is, you know, there's a sense of surprise and relief because we don't charge necessarily crazy rates.
We do have clients that are paying 25 and 30,000amonth.
But that's because of the scale of the work that we're doing.
The other thing that we do, which is a little different than your model, is all our client contracts are month to month.
And I think first of all, from a new business perspective, it seals the deal very quickly because they don't have to think about, this is going to put handcuffs on me for a year or six months.
And globally, this in particular helps us in the Middle east and places like that where commitment typically takes a longer time to happen.
But because we offer this service or this model, clients feel comfortable.
We do require the client to pay up front, so they're paying at the start of the month, not at the end of the month.
And, you know, so we try not to have.

And we've been pretty lucky over the years not to have any collection, you know, issues because they're paying up front and you know, you know, again, you know how costly it is to chase somebody who owes you money.
Absolutely.
Right.
So anyway, so.
All right, so that, that's, that's retainer.
What can you kind of rattle off the top three or top five clients that you have and what you're doing for them?
Yeah, absolutely.
And we offer a three month break clause for the same reason.
People think, well, I'm only committing for three months if it doesn't work out.
So I hear you.
And we cost in a similar way, a team rate.
I look at the blended team rate depending on the level of my time or more junior staff.
So it's not dissimilar.
And we charge fees at the beginning of the month and reimbursables at the end, just FYI.
Yes, absolutely.
Our top five clients.
So our largest current client is the city of Port Wentworth, which is, I know you do some stuff in obviously the government field on a much grander basis than we do.
We actually spent four years setting up the marketing department for Bryan county, which is part of the greater Savannah area where Hyundai are coming.

But great experience, great reputation.
Doing a similar thing for the city of Port Wentworth, which is another growing area.

We've worked with them.

Voice Festival.

Savannah is.

I mean it's closer than.
Yeah.

Yeah, okay.

But the, the new generation, I should call, I probably shouldn't say that.
They do value flexibility quite a lot.
But it's two way.

But that is variable.

Now that's quite expensive for me to outsource that.
So looking at another group that will have those resources in house, I do see some potential savings.
And also that would free up some time in terms of briefing and you know, the utilization of hours that the core, what I call the core team have Got it.

You said healthcare.
Right.

So I'm date.

Sure, sure.

Yes.

World.

We have opportunities in Atlanta.

It is, yeah.
You know, yeah.

So I'm being very candid.
Yeah.
No.

No, of course.
Very aware.

Right.

Okay.

We.

Okay.

We have some other internal things that we do to promote people.

The team had to be creative.
They had to come in from another way.
So.
So we, we attempt to do that twice a day.

Okay.

It's a lot of the basics of PR in the agency business.

The next.
The next thing we do is something called Creative Studio that meets twice a month now there.

You know, sometimes when a client, it's like on autopilot.
You know, we've been doing the same thing.
Or the team will say, oh, we tried that four years ago and it didn't work.
Well, you know, boy, the world has changed in four years.
